approaches.name: Hash set
approaches.idea: Walk the array once, adding each number to a set; if it is already there, you have found a duplicate.

approaches.name: Sort, then compare neighbours
approaches.idea: After sorting, equal values sit next to each other, so one pass comparing nums[i] with nums[i-1] finds a duplicate without extra memory.

approaches.name: Count letters in a 26-slot array
approaches.idea: Add 1 for each letter of s and subtract 1 for each letter of t; the strings are anagrams exactly when every count ends at zero.

approaches.name: One-pass hash map
approaches.idea: For each number, check whether target - number is already in a map of value → index; if not, store the current number and move on.

approaches.name: Letter-count key
approaches.idea: Use a tuple of 26 letter counts as the map key instead of the sorted word: counting is O(k) per word, sorting is O(k log k).

approaches.name: Bucket sort by frequency
approaches.idea: Count frequencies, then put each number in bucket[frequency] (frequencies are at most n); read buckets from the highest down until you have k numbers.

approaches.name: Min-heap of size k
approaches.idea: Count frequencies, then keep a heap of the k most frequent seen so far, popping the smallest whenever it grows past k.

approaches.name: Prefix and suffix products in the output array
approaches.idea: Fill the answer left to right with the product of everything before i, then sweep right to left multiplying in a running product of everything after i. Only O(1) extra besides the output, and no division.

approaches.name: One pass with row, column and box sets
approaches.idea: Visit each cell once and check its digit against a set for its row, its column and its 3×3 box (box index = (r // 3) * 3 + c // 3). With the board fixed at 9×9 this is effectively constant.

approaches.name: Length prefix
approaches.idea: Write each string as its length, a separator such as '#', then the string itself. Decoding reads the number, skips the separator and takes exactly that many characters, so any character can appear in the strings.

approaches.name: Hash set, counting only from sequence starts
approaches.idea: Put every number in a set. Only start counting at x when x - 1 is not in the set, then walk x + 1, x + 2, …; each number is visited a constant number of times overall.

approaches.name: Two pointers
approaches.idea: Move one pointer from each end, skipping non-alphanumeric characters and comparing lowercase letters, instead of building a cleaned copy of the string.

problem: Two Sum II Input Array Is Sorted

approaches.name: Two pointers
approaches.idea: Start at both ends: if the sum is too big move the right pointer left, if too small move the left pointer right. Sorting makes a hash map unnecessary.

approaches.name: Sort, then two pointers for each first number
approaches.idea: Sort, fix nums[i], and run a two-pointer search on the rest for pairs summing to -nums[i]. Skip equal neighbours to avoid duplicate triplets without a set.

approaches.name: Two pointers from the ends
approaches.idea: Start with the widest container and always move the shorter wall inward: moving the taller one can never give more water.

approaches.name: Two pointers with running maxima
approaches.idea: Keep leftMax and rightMax while moving pointers inward. Move the side with the smaller max: the water above that bar is fully decided by its own side's max.

approaches.name: Prefix and suffix maximum arrays
approaches.idea: Precompute the tallest bar to the left and right of every index; water at i is min(leftMax[i], rightMax[i]) - height[i].

problem: Best Time to Buy And Sell Stock

approaches.name: One pass tracking the lowest price
approaches.idea: Keep the cheapest price seen so far; at each day the best sale is price - cheapest. No need to try every pair.

approaches.name: Sliding window with last-seen index
approaches.idea: Store each character's last index. When a character repeats inside the window, jump the left edge straight past its previous position. Memory is bounded by the alphabet size.

approaches.name: Sliding window with the top count
approaches.idea: Keep letter counts for the window and the highest count seen. The window is valid while length - maxCount ≤ k; otherwise slide the left edge by one. The counts need only 26 slots.

approaches.name: Fixed-size window with 26 counts
approaches.idea: Slide a window of len(s1) over s2, adding the entering letter and removing the leaving one; track how many of the 26 counts match so each step is O(1).

approaches.name: Sliding window with a 'have vs need' counter
approaches.idea: Expand right until every needed character is covered (track how many are satisfied, not a full comparison), then shrink left while still valid, recording the smallest window.

approaches.name: Monotonic deque
approaches.idea: Keep indices in a deque with decreasing values: pop smaller values from the back before pushing, drop the front when it leaves the window. The front is always the maximum.

approaches.name: Stack
approaches.idea: Push opening brackets; on a closing bracket the top of the stack must be its match. The string is valid when the stack ends empty.

approaches.name: Store the minimum with each entry
approaches.idea: Push (value, min so far) pairs, or keep a second stack of minimums, so getMin reads the top instead of scanning.

approaches.name: Stack
approaches.idea: Push numbers; on an operator pop two, apply it (second popped is the left operand) and push the result.

approaches.name: Backtracking with open/close counts
approaches.idea: Only add '(' while open < n and ')' while close < open, so every string built is valid and nothing is generated then filtered.

approaches.name: Monotonic stack
approaches.idea: Keep a stack of indices still waiting for a warmer day. Each new temperature pops every colder day and fills in its wait; each index is pushed and popped once.

approaches.name: Sort by position, count arrival times
approaches.idea: Process cars from closest to the target. A car forms a new fleet only if it arrives later than the fleet ahead of it; otherwise it joins that fleet.

approaches.name: Monotonic stack
approaches.idea: Keep increasing heights on a stack. When a shorter bar arrives, pop taller bars and compute their rectangles: each popped bar extends back to its stored start index.

approaches.name: Iterative binary search
approaches.idea: Halve the search range each step with lo and hi pointers; a loop avoids the O(log n) stack of the recursive version.

approaches.name: One binary search over the flattened matrix
approaches.idea: Treat the matrix as one sorted list of m·n numbers: index i is row i // n, column i % n.

approaches.name: Binary search on the eating speed
approaches.idea: Speeds from 1 to max(piles) are monotonic: if speed s works, any faster speed works. Binary search for the slowest speed that finishes within h hours (m = the largest pile).

problem: Find Minimum In Rotated Sorted Array

approaches.name: Binary search against the right end
approaches.idea: If nums[mid] > nums[hi], the minimum is right of mid; otherwise it is at mid or to its left.

approaches.name: Binary search on the sorted half
approaches.idea: At each step one half is sorted. Check whether the target lies inside that half's range and discard the other half accordingly.

approaches.name: Map of lists + binary search on timestamps
approaches.idea: set appends (timestamps arrive increasing, so each list stays sorted); get binary-searches the key's list for the last timestamp ≤ the query.

approaches.name: Binary search on the partition
approaches.idea: Binary search how many elements the smaller array contributes to the left half; the partition is right when both left maxima are ≤ both right minima.

approaches.name: Iterative pointer reversal
approaches.idea: Walk the list keeping prev and curr, pointing curr.next back at prev. The recursive version uses O(n) stack.

approaches.name: Iterative merge with a dummy head
approaches.idea: Keep a tail pointer from a dummy node and splice in the smaller head each step, then attach whatever is left.

approaches.name: Find middle, reverse second half, merge
approaches.idea: Use slow/fast pointers to find the middle, reverse the second half in place, then interleave the two halves; no array of nodes needed.

problem: Remove Nth Node From End of List

approaches.name: Two pointers n apart, one pass
approaches.idea: Move a fast pointer n steps ahead of a slow one (starting at a dummy node); when fast reaches the end, slow is just before the node to remove.

approaches.name: Hash map from old node to copy
approaches.idea: First pass creates every copy in a map; second pass sets each copy's next and random through the map.

approaches.name: Interleave copies in the original list
approaches.idea: Insert each copy right after its original (A → A' → B → B'), set copy.random = original.random.next, then unweave the two lists. No map needed.

approaches.name: Digit-by-digit with a carry
approaches.idea: Walk both lists together adding digits and the carry into a new list; continue while either list or the carry remains. Only the result list takes memory.

approaches.name: Floyd's slow and fast pointers
approaches.idea: Move one pointer one step and another two steps; they meet if and only if there is a cycle. No visited set needed.

approaches.name: Floyd's cycle detection on indices
approaches.idea: Treat i → nums[i] as a linked list; the duplicate is where the cycle begins. Find the meeting point, then restart one pointer from 0 and step both until they meet.

approaches.name: Hash map + doubly linked list
approaches.idea: The map finds a node in O(1); the list keeps usage order so moving a node to the front and evicting from the back are both O(1).

approaches.name: Min-heap of the list heads
approaches.idea: Keep one node from each list in a heap; pop the smallest, append it, push its next. Merging lists in pairs (divide and conquer) is also O(n log k).

approaches.name: Iterative group reversal
approaches.idea: Check that k nodes remain, reverse them in place, reconnect to the previous group's tail, and move on; recursion would use O(n/k) stack.

approaches.name: DFS swapping children
approaches.idea: Swap the left and right child of every node, recursively or with an explicit stack; h is the tree's height.

approaches.name: DFS
approaches.idea: depth(node) = 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)); the stack only ever holds one root-to-leaf path.

approaches.name: One DFS returning height
approaches.idea: Each call returns its height and updates the best diameter with left height + right height, instead of recomputing heights for every node.

approaches.name: One DFS returning height or 'unbalanced'
approaches.idea: Return -1 as soon as any subtree is unbalanced, otherwise its height, so each node is visited once instead of recomputing heights top-down.

approaches.name: Simultaneous DFS
approaches.idea: Two trees are the same if the roots match and both pairs of subtrees are the same; stop at the first mismatch.

approaches.name: DFS with a same-tree check at each node
approaches.idea: At every node of the main tree, run the same-tree check against the subtree.

approaches.name: Serialize both trees and search the string
approaches.idea: Serialize each tree in preorder with null markers and delimiters, then search for the smaller string in the larger with KMP or Z-algorithm.

problem: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree

approaches.name: Walk down using BST order
approaches.idea: From the root: if both values are smaller go left, if both larger go right, otherwise this node is the split point. A loop needs no stack.

approaches.name: BFS level by level
approaches.idea: Process the queue in batches of its current length; each batch is one level.

approaches.name: BFS keeping the last node per level
approaches.idea: Do a level-order traversal and record the last node of each level (or DFS right-first, recording the first node at each new depth).

problem: Count Good Nodes In Binary Tree

approaches.name: DFS carrying the path maximum
approaches.idea: Pass the largest value seen on the path down; a node is good when its value ≥ that maximum.

approaches.name: DFS with lower and upper bounds
approaches.idea: Each node must lie strictly between bounds inherited from its ancestors; checking only parent-child pairs misses deeper violations.

problem: Kth Smallest Element In a Bst

approaches.name: Iterative inorder, stop at k
approaches.idea: Inorder visits a BST in sorted order; use an explicit stack and stop after the kth pop instead of collecting every value.

problem: Construct Binary Tree From Preorder And Inorder Traversal

approaches.name: Recursion with an inorder index map
approaches.idea: Map each value to its inorder index so finding the root's position is O(1), and pass index ranges instead of slicing lists (slicing makes it O(n²)).

approaches.name: DFS returning the best downward gain
approaches.idea: Each call returns node + max(0, best child gain) and updates the answer with node + both children's gains (negative gains clipped to 0).

approaches.name: Preorder with null markers
approaches.idea: Write values in preorder with a marker for missing children; rebuild by reading tokens in the same order with an index or iterator.

problem: Kth Largest Element In a Stream

approaches.name: Min-heap of size k
approaches.idea: Keep only the k largest values in a min-heap; its top is the kth largest. Each add is one push and at most one pop, never a full sort.

approaches.name: Max-heap
approaches.idea: Pop the two heaviest, push back their difference if non-zero; a heap avoids re-sorting after every smash.

approaches.name: Quickselect on distance
approaches.idea: Partition around a pivot distance as in quicksort, but only recurse into the side containing the kth position. O(n) on average (O(n²) worst case).

approaches.name: Max-heap of size k
approaches.idea: Keep the k closest points seen so far in a max-heap keyed by distance; pop the farthest when it grows past k.

problem: Kth Largest Element In An Array

approaches.name: Quickselect
approaches.idea: Partition around a pivot and only continue into the side that contains index n - k. O(n) on average; a random pivot keeps the worst case unlikely.

approaches.name: Min-heap of size k
approaches.idea: Keep the k largest values in a min-heap; the top at the end is the answer.

approaches.name: Count the most frequent task
approaches.idea: With maxCount the highest frequency and tied the number of tasks sharing it, the answer is max(len(tasks), (maxCount - 1) * (n + 1) + tied). No simulation needed.

approaches.name: Heap over each followee's latest tweet
approaches.idea: Store each user's tweets newest last. For the feed, push each followee's latest tweet into a heap and pop 10 times, pushing that user's previous tweet each time, instead of sorting every tweet.

approaches.name: Two heaps
approaches.idea: A max-heap holds the smaller half and a min-heap the larger half, kept within one element of each other; the median is read from the tops.

approaches.name: Backtracking (include / exclude)
approaches.idea: For each element choose to include it or not; every leaf is a subset. There are 2ⁿ subsets, so this is optimal.

approaches.name: Backtracking from the current index
approaches.idea: Recurse on the same index (reuse allowed) or move to the next one; stop once the remaining target goes negative. Sorting lets you break early.

approaches.name: Backtracking with a used flag or swaps
approaches.idea: Pick each unused number for the next position; swapping in place avoids copying lists. There are n! permutations, so this is optimal.

approaches.name: Sort, then skip equal neighbours
approaches.idea: After choosing to skip a value, skip all its copies too, so duplicates are never generated and no set of results is needed.

approaches.name: Sort, backtrack, skip duplicates
approaches.idea: At each depth skip a value equal to the previous one at that depth, and stop when a number exceeds the remaining target.

approaches.name: DFS from each cell, marking the path in place
approaches.idea: Mark a cell as visited by overwriting it during the DFS and restore it on the way back, instead of keeping a visited set. After the first step there are only 3 directions to try (L = word length).

approaches.name: Backtracking with a palindrome table
approaches.idea: Precompute isPal[i][j] with DP so each palindrome check is O(1), then backtrack over cut positions.

problem: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number

approaches.name: Backtracking over digits
approaches.idea: Each digit maps to 3 or 4 letters; build one letter per depth. The output itself has up to 4ⁿ strings, so this is optimal.

approaches.name: Backtracking with column and diagonal sets
approaches.idea: Place one queen per row; sets for columns, r + c and r - c make each safety check O(1) instead of scanning the board.

approaches.name: Trie nodes with child maps
approaches.idea: Each operation walks one node per character of the word (n = word length); storage grows with the total characters inserted.

problem: Design Add And Search Words Data Structure

approaches.name: Trie with DFS on '.'
approaches.idea: Add is a normal trie insert. Search follows one child per letter and branches into every child only at '.', so plain words cost O(word length).

approaches.name: Trie of words + one DFS per cell
approaches.idea: Build a trie of all words and search the board once, following trie edges; remove words from the trie once found so later searches prune early. Much faster than running Word Search for each word.

approaches.name: Flood fill (DFS or BFS)
approaches.idea: Scan the grid; each time you meet unvisited land, count an island and sink all its connected land so it is never counted again.

approaches.name: DFS or BFS with an old → new map
approaches.idea: Create each copy the first time you meet a node and look it up in the map afterwards, so cycles don't cause infinite loops.

approaches.name: Flood fill returning area
approaches.idea: DFS from each unvisited land cell returns 1 + the areas of its neighbours; mark cells visited so each is counted once.

approaches.name: Search inward from both oceans
approaches.idea: Run DFS/BFS from every border cell of each ocean, moving only to neighbours at least as high. Cells reached from both oceans are the answer. Searching from every cell separately is O((m·n)²).

approaches.name: Mark border-connected O's first
approaches.idea: DFS from every 'O' on the border and mark it safe; then flip every remaining 'O' to 'X' and restore the safe ones.

approaches.name: Multi-source BFS
approaches.idea: Put every rotten orange in the queue at minute 0 and spread level by level; the number of levels is the answer, if no fresh orange is left.

approaches.name: Multi-source BFS from all gates
approaches.idea: Start BFS from every gate at once; the first time a room is reached is its shortest distance, so each cell is visited once instead of once per gate.

approaches.name: Topological sort (Kahn's algorithm)
approaches.idea: Repeatedly take courses with no remaining prerequisites; if every course gets taken there is no cycle. DFS with three colours works too.

approaches.name: Topological sort (Kahn's algorithm)
approaches.idea: Same as Course Schedule, recording the order courses leave the queue; return empty if some course is never freed.

approaches.name: Union-find
approaches.idea: Add edges one by one; the first edge whose endpoints already share a root closes a cycle. With path compression and union by rank each operation is effectively O(1) (inverse Ackermann).

problem: Number of Connected Components In An Undirected Graph

approaches.name: Union-find
approaches.idea: Start with V components and subtract one for every edge that joins two different roots. DFS over an adjacency list is equally fast.

approaches.name: Edge count + union-find
approaches.idea: A tree has exactly n - 1 edges; with that checked, it's a tree if no edge joins two nodes that are already connected.

approaches.name: BFS with wildcard patterns
approaches.idea: Index words by patterns like 'h*t' so neighbours are found by pattern lookup instead of comparing every pair of words (k = word length). Bidirectional BFS is faster in practice.

approaches.name: Hierholzer's algorithm
approaches.idea: Sort each airport's destinations, DFS using each ticket once, and add an airport to the route after its tickets are used up; reverse at the end. No backtracking needed.

problem: Min Cost to Connect All Points

approaches.name: Prim's algorithm with an array
approaches.idea: The graph is complete, so skip building all n² edges: keep each point's cheapest distance to the tree in an array and add the closest point each round.

approaches.name: Dijkstra with a min-heap
approaches.idea: Pop the closest unsettled node and relax its edges; the answer is the largest settled distance, or -1 if some node is never reached.

approaches.name: Dijkstra on the maximum height
approaches.idea: Always expand the reachable cell with the lowest elevation; the answer is the highest elevation popped before reaching the corner.

approaches.name: Topological sort over letters
approaches.idea: Compare each adjacent pair of words to find the first differing letter, which gives one edge; then topologically sort the letters. Watch for a word followed by its own prefix (invalid). n = total characters.

approaches.name: Bellman-Ford for k + 1 rounds
approaches.idea: Relax every edge k + 1 times, each round working from a copy of the previous round's prices so a route never uses more stops than allowed.

approaches.name: Two running variables
approaches.idea: ways(i) = ways(i-1) + ways(i-2), so keep only the last two values. Plain recursion without memoisation is O(2ⁿ).

approaches.name: Bottom-up DP with two variables
approaches.idea: The cost to reach step i is cost[i] + min of the two before it; keep only the last two values.

approaches.name: DP with two variables
approaches.idea: best(i) = max(best(i-1), best(i-2) + nums[i]); keep only the last two values instead of a table or an unmemoised recursion.

approaches.name: House Robber twice
approaches.idea: The first and last houses can't both be robbed, so take the better of robbing houses 0..n-2 and 1..n-1 with the O(1)-space House Robber.

approaches.name: Expand around each centre
approaches.idea: Try all 2n - 1 centres (letters and gaps) and expand while the ends match. Same speed as the DP table without its O(n²) memory.

approaches.name: Manacher's algorithm
approaches.idea: Reuses palindrome radii mirrored around the rightmost palindrome found so far, so each character is expanded past only once.

approaches.name: Expand around each centre
approaches.idea: From each of the 2n - 1 centres, expand while the ends match and count one palindrome per step.

approaches.name: Manacher's algorithm
approaches.idea: Compute every centre's palindrome radius in linear time; the count is the sum of (radius + 1) / 2 over the transformed string.

approaches.name: DP with two variables
approaches.idea: ways(i) adds ways(i-1) if s[i] is 1–9 and ways(i-2) if s[i-1..i] is 10–26; keep only the last two values.

approaches.name: Bottom-up DP over amounts
approaches.idea: dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a - coin]) over the n coins, for every amount up to t. Greedy picking of the largest coin fails on inputs like [1, 3, 4] with amount 6.

approaches.name: Track the running max and min
approaches.idea: A negative number turns the smallest product into the largest, so keep both the max and min product ending at each index.

approaches.name: DP over prefixes
approaches.idea: dp[i] is true if some dictionary word ends at i and dp[i - len(word)] is true (n = string length, m words of length up to k). Plain recursion without memoisation is exponential.

approaches.name: Patience sorting with binary search
approaches.idea: Keep tails[i] = the smallest tail of any increasing subsequence of length i + 1; binary-search where each number goes. The length of tails is the answer.

approaches.name: DP over pairs
approaches.idea: lis[i] = 1 + max(lis[j]) for j < i with nums[j] < nums[i].

approaches.name: 1-D subset-sum DP
approaches.idea: t = half the total. Keep a boolean array of reachable sums and update it right to left for each number so each number is used once (a set of sums works too).

approaches.name: One-row DP
approaches.idea: Each cell is the one above plus the one to its left, so a single row updated in place is enough. The binomial formula C(m+n-2, m-1) is faster still.

approaches.name: DP keeping one row
approaches.idea: Row i only needs row i - 1, so keep one row over the shorter string plus a variable for the diagonal.

problem: Best Time to Buy And Sell Stock With Cooldown

approaches.name: Three-state machine
approaches.idea: Track the best profit while holding, just sold, and resting; each day's three values come from the previous day's.

approaches.name: 1-D DP, coins in the outer loop
approaches.idea: Loop over coins outside and amounts inside so each combination is counted once, not once per order.

approaches.name: Reduce to subset-sum DP
approaches.idea: If P is the plus-set, sum(P) = (total + target) / 2, so count subsets with that sum using a 1-D DP. Trying every sign is O(2ⁿ).

approaches.name: DP keeping one row
approaches.idea: dp[j] says whether s1[:i] and s2[:j] can form s3[:i+j]; each row only needs the previous one.

problem: Longest Increasing Path In a Matrix

approaches.name: DFS with memoisation
approaches.idea: The longest path from a cell never changes, so cache it; each cell is computed once. No visited set is needed because paths strictly increase.

approaches.name: 1-D DP
approaches.idea: dp[j] counts ways to form t[:j]; for each character of s, update j from right to left: dp[j] += dp[j-1] when s[i] == t[j-1].

approaches.name: DP keeping one row
approaches.idea: Each cell is 1 + min(insert, delete, replace), or the diagonal when characters match; keep one row and the diagonal value.

approaches.name: Interval DP on the last balloon burst
approaches.idea: Pad with 1s and let dp[l][r] be the best for the open interval; choosing which balloon bursts last splits it into independent halves.

approaches.name: DP over string and pattern positions
approaches.idea: dp[i][j] says whether s[i:] matches p[j:]; '*' either skips the pair x* or consumes one matching character. Plain recursion without a cache is exponential.

approaches.name: Kadane's algorithm
approaches.idea: Keep the best sum ending here: extend it with the current number, or restart at the current number if the running sum went negative.

approaches.name: Greedy goal pointer
approaches.idea: Walk from the end, moving the goal to i whenever i + nums[i] reaches it; you can win if the goal reaches index 0.

approaches.name: Greedy BFS by ranges
approaches.idea: Treat each jump as a level: track the farthest index reachable from the current range and jump when you pass the range's end.

approaches.name: One pass with a running tank
approaches.idea: If total gas < total cost there is no answer. Otherwise, whenever the tank goes negative, the next station becomes the new start.

approaches.name: Counts + smallest card first
approaches.idea: Count cards, then from the smallest remaining value build a group of groupSize consecutive values, decrementing counts; any missing card means false.

problem: Merge Triplets to Form Target Triplet

approaches.name: One pass, ignore triplets that overshoot
approaches.idea: Skip any triplet with a value above the target; among the rest, check that each target position is matched by some triplet.

approaches.name: Last index + one pass
approaches.idea: Record each letter's last index (26 slots), extend the current part's end to the furthest last index seen, and cut when i reaches it.

approaches.name: Greedy range of open counts
approaches.idea: Track the lowest and highest possible open count; '*' widens the range. Fail if high drops below 0, clamp low at 0, and succeed if low ends at 0.

approaches.name: One pass: before, merge, after
approaches.idea: Copy intervals ending before the new one, merge every overlapping interval into it, then copy the rest. No sorting needed because the input is sorted.

approaches.name: Sort by start, then merge
approaches.idea: After sorting, each interval either overlaps the last merged one (extend its end) or starts a new one.

approaches.name: Sort by end, keep greedily
approaches.idea: Keep the interval that ends earliest and remove anything overlapping it; this leaves the most room for later intervals.

approaches.name: Sort by start, compare neighbours
approaches.idea: After sorting, an overlap can only happen between consecutive meetings.

approaches.name: Sorted starts and ends, two pointers
approaches.idea: Sort start and end times separately; a start before the earliest unfinished end needs a new room. A min-heap of end times is equally fast.

problem: Minimum Interval to Include Each Query

approaches.name: Sort both, sweep with a min-heap
approaches.time: O(n log n + q log q)
approaches.idea: Process queries in increasing order, pushing intervals that have started (keyed by size) and popping ones that have ended; the heap top answers the query.

approaches.name: Transpose, then reverse each row
approaches.idea: Swapping across the diagonal and then mirroring each row rotates the matrix 90° clockwise in place, with no copy.

approaches.name: Shrinking boundaries
approaches.idea: Keep top, bottom, left and right bounds; walk one side at a time and move that bound inward. Only O(1) extra besides the output, with no visited grid.

approaches.name: First row and column as markers
approaches.idea: Use row 0 and column 0 to record which rows and columns to zero, with one extra flag for column 0 itself, instead of separate sets.

fixedSize: the input is one number, and its digit-square sums quickly drop below a few hundred

approaches.name: Floyd's cycle detection
approaches.idea: Apply the digit-square sum with a slow and a fast pointer; they meet at 1 if the number is happy, or elsewhere in a cycle. No seen set needed.

approaches.name: Carry from the last digit
approaches.idea: Turn trailing 9s into 0s and add one to the first non-9 digit; only an all-9s number needs a new leading 1.

approaches.name: Fast exponentiation (iterative)
approaches.idea: Square x and halve n each step, multiplying the result in when the current bit of n is 1; handle negative n by inverting x.

approaches.name: Grade-school multiplication into one array
approaches.idea: The product of digits i and j lands at positions i + j and i + j + 1 of an array of length m + n; add into it and carry as you go.

approaches.name: Point counts + diagonal lookup
approaches.idea: Count each point. For a query, treat every stored point that makes a diagonal with it as the opposite corner and multiply the counts of the other two corners.

approaches.name: XOR everything
approaches.idea: a ^ a = 0 and a ^ 0 = a, so XOR-ing every number leaves only the one that appears once. No hash set needed.

approaches.name: Clear the lowest set bit
approaches.idea: n & (n - 1) removes the lowest 1 bit, so the loop runs once per set bit (at most 32 times).

approaches.name: DP from the number shifted right
approaches.idea: bits[i] = bits[i >> 1] + (i & 1): i has the same bits as i // 2 plus its last bit. Counting each number separately is O(n log n).

approaches.name: 32 shifts
approaches.idea: Take the last bit of n, shift it into the result from the other side, and repeat 32 times.

approaches.name: XOR or the sum formula
approaches.idea: n(n + 1)/2 minus the array's sum is the missing number (or XOR all indices and values). No sorting or set needed.

approaches.name: XOR for the sum, AND-shift for the carry
approaches.idea: a ^ b adds without carrying and (a & b) << 1 is the carry; repeat until the carry is 0 (at most 32 rounds; mask to 32 bits in Python).

fixedSize: the input is one 32-bit number with at most 10 digits

approaches.name: Pop and push digits with an overflow check
approaches.idea: Take digits with % 10 and build the result with * 10, checking against the 32-bit limits before each push instead of converting to a string.
